Century Arms Apparatus Pistols: The Roller-Locked Dream Makers 

By Will Dabbs MD

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:00
Instaread

I’ve always been a gun nerd. I honestly don’t know why. I have pretty normal parents, and my brothers aren’t particularly weird. However, for as long as I can remember I have been simply smitten with firearms. Maybe I was swapped at birth. I can only imagine what that other guy must be going through…

I came of age in the 1980’s. I was too young to avail myself of cheap machine guns and too broke for much else. Back in the day, the golden ring was the HK MP5. I watched the Iranian Embassy takedown in London in 1980 as it happened on the news. Those black-clad SAS operators packing MP5’s as they abseiled down the front of that building were about the coolest things I had ever seen. 

Advertisement — Continue Reading Below

I drooled over these weapons in such big screen classics as Die Hard, Predator, and Navy SEALs. I would have drunk bathwater to land an MP5 of my own. Alas, the prejudices of the uninitiated and a tragic lack of funds conspired to keep us apart. 

And thus things languished for literally decades. The gun collection wheezed along in dribs and drabs as I could scrape up a little cash over and above rent and diapers. And then Century Arms finally heard my plaintive cries from the wilderness. Their Apparatus Pistols were the key to a literal lifelong dream.

Origin Story

I neither know nor care why they call it an Apparatus Pistol. Reality is that these guns are the closest anyone will come on this side of the pond to a real-deal Oberndorf HK SMG (remember, HK exports are different even though they are HK). For a gun nerd who is serious about his craft, this is Candyland.

Our tale begins back during World War 2 with the MG42 belt-fed general purpose machinegun. The Germans fielded the previous MG34 in, you guessed it, 1934, but it was expensive to make and a bit finicky in the filthy sorts of spaces where soldiers live. The MG42 was designed to be inexpensive and unkillable. 

Advertisement — Continue Reading Below

The guys who got tagged to bodge up the MG42 had never before built a firearm. The company had previously produced pressed steel railway lanterns. As a result, they had few preconceived notions regarding what a machinegun should look like. 

They adapted the mechanism from an industrial pile driver and transformed it into a firearm. The gun was recoil-operated via a novel roller-delayed blowback system. In this case a pair of fairly unremarkable roller bearings set into the bolt assembly cammed into corresponding slots in the bolt face and slowed separation down just enough to allow pressures to drop to safe levels. The end result was cheap to make and crazy reliable. It also cycled those big honking 7.92x57mm rounds at a blistering rate of around 1,200 rpm. The MG42 remains in series production as the MG3 chambered in 7.62x51mm NATO even today.

As WW2 ground to its bloody terminus, the Germans adapted this roller-delayed system to the StG45 assault rifle. This gun fired the revolutionary 7.92x33mm kurz round of the MP44 Sturmgewehr but was cheaper to make. It had not progressed beyond prototype stage by war’s end.

The Mauser engineers who had been working on the StG45 took their drawings to Spain and adapted the gun into the Spanish CETME battle rifle. Once Germany had regained its footing, they went back home and formed Heckler and Koch. The CETME evolved into the G3 that served for decades as the standard service rifle of the West German Bundeswehr. It was also a middle finger back to the Belgians who were being difficult about the FAL.

HK shrunk the G3 action down to accept 9mm components and created the MP5 submachine gun. Along the way, they also built the gun in 5.56x45mm and 7.62x39mm as well. The MP5 first saw service with West German border police in 1966.

These HK guns were arguably the world’s first modular combat weapons. The receivers were not interchangeable, but they were quite similar. In 1974, the basic 9mm MP5 was fitted with an integrally suppressed barrel assembly that was ported to drop the velocity of standard 9mm ball ammo down into the subsonic range. Two years later, HK shrunk the gun down for some Middle Eastern potentate to create the stubby MP5K concealable version. In 1991, the MP5K was fitted with a longer barrel and side-folding stock to become the MP5K PDW. 

Advertisement — Continue Reading Below

None of that mattered to me. Those guns might just as well have been on the moon. It seemed I would never even see one in the flesh. Nowadays, however, thanks to Century Arms we can land most of that stuff at fairly reasonable prices at our local gun emporium.

Details

All of these weapons are sold as handguns. They are produced in Turkey on HK-licensed machinery. The original HK versions are castrated to conform with German export laws. In addition to being just crazy expensive, the HK94, as an example, lacks a flapper magazine release and has its fire control unit held in place with a single pin. The Century versions use two pins like the GI originals. Normal people don’t care, but geeks like me do.

As has been a glorious boon, the National Firearms Act transfer taxes for short-barreled weapons and sound suppressors has dropped to zero. The onerous registration requirement remains, but doing away with that unconstitutional tax has made NFA registration hugely more appealing. As we explore the Century stable, I’ll walk you through how to register these guns and make them factory-correct.

Variety is the Spice of Life

The AP5M is the semiauto version of the stubby MP5K with a 4.5-inch barrel. This variant lacks the forward vertical broomstick grip but is otherwise a spitting image for the gun used by the T-1000 in Terminator 2. The AP5M comes with a solid buttcap equipped with a sling swivel.

Advertisement — Continue Reading Below

Adding the foregrip makes the gun an AOW (Any Other Weapon) in the eyes of Uncle Sam. AOWs are so stupid they do not warrant exploration. Suffice to say, after 1 January 2026 just drop a BATF Form 1 via their e-Forms site, and you can put whatever you want on the front of this gun. All of these 9mm AP5 weapons come with two standard steel 30-round magazines.

The AP5P is the basic chassis of the MP5K PDW with a 5.5-inch barrel. The MP5K PDW was designed specially to equip NATO aviators. The AP5P is identical to the AP5M, except that it has a stubby bit of threaded tri-lug barrel up front. Add your now $0 taxed cans accordingly.

To build up an MP5K PDW, register the gun as a short-barreled rifle and then add the vertical foregrip and a side-folding Choate buttstock. Keep in mind that the mounting geometry is different for the K-model and the standard MP5. Just make sure you order the right stock.

The AP5 is the semiauto pistol version of the standard MP5. This gun sports an 8.9-inch barrel and a buttcap. The barrel is threaded and includes a tri-lug suppressor mount. 

Once you have this gun registered, installation of any of several fixed or collapsible buttstocks is just plug and play. Original German sliding stocks are astronomically expensive. However, Turkish imports are cheaper, and Magpul offers their own proprietary design that runs about $150. 

The AP5SD is a clone of the uber-sexy MP5SD that includes the same 5.5-inch barrel of the AP5P hidden underneath an open-ended aluminum fake suppressor. The AP5SD comes with the standard round rubber tubular handgun of the GI gun. This model is available with either a buttcap or a nice collapsible pistol stabilizing brace.

The fake suppressor screws right off. It is an easy thing to thread on any appropriate live pistol can in its place so long as it will fit into the forearm. However, as the barrel is not ported, regular ball rounds will remain supersonic. To get that super-quiet MP5SD performance will require heavy 147-grain subsonic ammo.

Advertisement — Continue Reading Below

Proper Power

The AP53 is basically the same gun as the AP5 only chambered in 5.56mm. The AP53 includes an 8.3-inch barrel. The muzzle is threaded 1/2×28 should you have a 5.56mm suppressor handy. The same buttstocks that fit the AP5 will drop onto the AP53. The gun comes with two translucent polymer 30-round magazines that snap together jungle-fashion. 

The AP51 is the same weapon now chambered for the earth-shaking 7.62x51mm cartridge. The barrel is 8.5 inches long and threaded 5/8×24 for a suppressor. The AP51 also comes with two polymer 20-round mags that snap together.

Both the AP51 and AP53 come with a buttcap. Once registered, they will take collapsible stocks as well. Be advised, the AP51 stock mounts with two pins rather than one, so it demands a G3-specific stock. However, these stocks can be found on the surplus market and are a bit cheaper than the MP5 sort as a result.

All of these weapons come with a sling, a nice cleaning kit, and an excellent aluminum scope mount. They all use a common manual of arms that includes the legendary “HK slap” to drop the bolt over a fresh mag. That’s a bit slower than the same drill with an M4 but way sexier.

Ruminations

Over time, I have accumulated all of these weapons. Mine have been unflinchingly reliable and unnaturally accurate. H&K was floating barrels before it was cool. The 9mm versions run like sewing machines. The rifle-caliber versions produce a muzzle flash that is visible from the International Space Station. Slip the flash suppressor off of the AP51, and it will burn the hair off of your chest. To Century Arms I can only say–sincerely and from my heart—thanks.
